segments.text: Hey guys. So, a while back I made a video about my journey into the world of coding, how I taught myself how to code,
and then that led to me breaking into the quant industry. But now, 5 years later on YouTube, I want to talk about
what the journey in the quant industry is like, where I'm going now, and how I broke in to begin with. So, I want to
start with my experience in university. That's where everything really started. I went to Queens University in Kingston,
Ontario, and I studied commerce as my major. I didn't come from a computer science background and I studied in
Canada. That's where Queens University is at. The town that I was in, Kingston was essentially 80% students throughout
the entire year. And at the time, I really thought I wanted to go into investment banking. I won the national
investment banking competition. I was clearly dedicated. I studied hard, got the best grades that I could. But to put
it simply, I just was not a culture fit for that industry. At least that's how I felt after interviewing there and
working an internship there during my second year of university. Now, I already proved to myself that I was good
enough for it by winning the national investment banking competition, which was the top award in the space at the
time. But no firm really wanted somebody who had a scruffy beard, long hair, and who didn't live and breathe hockey or
basketball. At least that was my impression interviewing the space. So instead of pursuing what I thought would
make me the most money, I decided to pursue what I was interested in and that was cryptocurrency. During my last year
of university, all my friends had internships lined up, had big career gigs in consulting, the big four,
Mckenzie, investment banking, Lazards, Goldman Sachs, all that stuff. And I had nothing lined up. All I had was a really
strong interest in cryptocurrency, which at the time was super hot, but has since wavered a little. What I decided to do
with that interest was stop waiting for employers to find me and just take my interest to an employer. So I reached
out to what was the largest cryptocurrency derivatives exchange in the world at the time, BitMEX. And I did
so by just first hitting up the research department via Twitter. I used to read their articles all the time. And before
interviewing, they said, "We're down to interview you. Just build us something and let's talk about it in an interview
setting." That was my gateway into the research team. So, I essentially put together a PowerPoint about a topic I
found interesting, presented it to the head of research over a Zoom call, and a week later, he said, "All right, you're
in." So, fast forward, they offered me an internship position where they sponsored my living and paid me a pretty
decent intern salary to work in their Hong Kong office. At the time, it was like 30 people, super rugged, like super
entrepreneurial vibes. the flight was paid. Uh the board as in the living was paid. And I would be sitting in a small
office in the middle of Hong Kong, you know, with those group of 30 people. Literally like a billionaire sitting on
my right and a billionaire on my left and then the dev team and then like a bit of HR and the research team and
maybe the structured products team. Now between research and structured products work, when I had spare time, I started
coding. In particular, I used Q/KDB to complete tasks that were rudimentary and that could be easily automated.
Remember, this was before AI even existed. And out of every language possible, they were using probably the
most esoteric and just crazy to understand one out there. You see, most languages C++, Python, they're all
public. There's a committee that develops them. But Q is a private programming language. It's developed by
KX Systems. And in order to use the 64-bit version of that language, you had to pay Q. For those that don't know,
it's built on top of K, which is built on top of APL. It's a very tur array oriented programming language created by
a man named Arthur Whitney. Now, I never understood how people can go about creating programming languages to this
extent. Like Q is a super small programming language. It fits in L1 cache. These people, they're just next
level. But coming back to the topic at hand, it's interesting that I grew a interest in Q/KDB because I was never interested in
programming while in school and I think that's because I was really intimidated by how much further ahead my friends
were in languages like Python than I was and so I never made an active effort to just go and learn. And that fear
prevented me from ever taking on any coding related classes in school. But here I was in a new country and a new
language picking up one of the most tur programming languages in the world and it didn't really seem intimidating at
all. Over time, I slowly started doing more work related to Q and KDB. I built an internal database to track BitMEX
addresses and transactions that was used by the research team to gain a sense of their onchain footprint. This was doable
because BitMEX addresses were all vanity addresses, meaning they were generated to start with distinct characters which
were 3bmex. I got to a point where I started coding for the majority of my time at the organization and I slowly but surely
fell in love with the unique programming language which was Q and KDB. I actually felt quite cool because none of my
friends were coding in that language. I was even able to convince the organization to pay for classes that
would teach me more intermediate and advanced levels of Q and KDB. So I really got to a point where I wanted to
lean in and dedicate more time to coding. The head of risk also noticed that my proficiency and interest in the
language was increasing and essentially offered me a position on his team. Now, at the time, I was in a graduate
rotational program going between research, structured products, and other divisions, and that didn't really allow
me to move into a programming related role. So, I just needed to take a bet. I needed to take a bet on whether the head
of risk had enough pull in the organization to convince the COO that I should leave the graduate rotational
program and join the riskbased development team. Now, I decided to take that bet because my newfound level of
excitement had just outstripped and outweighed the mundaness of hopping between research and structured
products. Unfortunately for me, or maybe fortunately given what it resulted in, the COO essentially told me that I will
never code, that I should never want to aspire to be a software engineer, and that I would be fired if I did not take
the role as a structured products analyst at the end of the graduate rotational program. So the next day I
had a discussion with the head of structured products. I told him, "Listen, dude, I'm not interested in
this work." At the time, I essentially quit because I was too green to formally resign and do it the right way. So
around 2 hours after letting him know that, I was essentially pulled back into the office by the COO and formally
fired. At the time, there was a lot of political upheaval in Hong Kong. There were rumors going around about the
cough, if you know what I mean. So my dad told me, "Get the f out of Hong Kong. Come live with us for the time
being." And so that's what I did. I left Hong Kong, but I took my passion for software engineering and development
with me. Now, I wasn't sure what I needed to be doing. I would knew that I was interested in financial markets
because I lived and breathed them during my time at BitMX in Hong Kong, but I knew that the job market for Q and KDB
plus developers was limited to essentially like the top 10 15% of Q developers. They were making like
upwards of 500K. And so that was super competitive, especially given just how niche the language was. What I ended up
doing was doing my research and I found that C++ was a language to learn if you wanted a software engineering career in
anything markets related. So I essentially locked myself in my parents' guest room, bought C++, a beginner's
guide, and went to work starting there for 7 to 8 hours a day. Now, at the time, there was naturally a lot of
guessing because there wasn't anybody online that was talking about careers in software engineering, in particular in
the quanter finance space. So, part of my journey was what inspired me to create this channel, a channel that I
wish I had available back when I was learning from scratch. My studying was essentially all over the place because I
didn't have that virtual mentor. I didn't have any guidance. I didn't even have Chad GPT to like remotely help me
guess what was important. And so my learning was all over the place. And most of every minute I spent I spent
studying naturally. I bought some more books, bought some books on GameDev. I built a little 2D C++ cavetory game via
an online video tutorials on YouTube. And I went through what we all go through, learn cpp.com. I picked up, you
know, various books on database technologies. And essentially, I tried to make myself as much of a professional
C++ developer as I could as an amateur C++ enjoyer. I remember there was actually this like tadada moment when I
spoke to a friend of mine who at the time worked for Akuna Capital uh about learning C++. He was in a role that was
kind of like a hybrid between a trader and a developer. He's now working at Citadel Security, super cracked, super
smart guy. And his encouragement at such a formative part of my journey was actually one of the reasons why I
decided to keep going. You see, I remember walking him through my learning plan, and he naturally asked me like a
couple of questions. For example, what's the difference between a reference and a pointer? And despite that being so
simple looking back at it, when we were going through those concepts, and it wasn't just that, to be fair, he was
surprised at how quickly I was able to pick up those distinctions. Now, this isn't to toot my own horn, to say, "Oh,
look at me. I know the difference between a reference and a pointer." It's just to emphasize the importance of
having somebody in your corner to give you that shot in the arm or correct your direction when needed. [snorts] Around 2
months in, that's when another friend of mine that works at Meta on the DevOps side told me that I need to start
picking up lead code because that would be one of the gates I would need to pass if I wanted to land a role in the space.
Now, this was where I took the biggest gut punch because I remember my first question being the rearrange bits or not rearrange, it was
reverse bits uh in a given integer. So, you have a 32-bit integer and they wanted you to reverse the bits in that
integer. And I was just totally devastated by that question. I think I spent two hours on that problem and I
asked myself, what the hell was I doing these last two months if I can't even reverse bits? I was embarrassed and
honestly I felt really really deflated. But instead of just quitting, I reminded myself why I was doing this to begin
with and just decided to look at the answers. I then set a rule for myself. Essentially any easy if I spent more
than 30 minutes on it and any medium, if I spent more than 40 minutes on it, I would just straight up look at the
answer. I try to learn the topic cuz clearly I didn't know it well enough. And then I would reapply that topic on
that question and several other related questions. A week or two after that regrouped with a friend of mine, the
same person you know from DevOps at Meta and we did a mock interview together. And I remember doing quite decently. He
gave me the problem of determining the count of nested parenthesis, the one where you need to use a stack to go
about doing it and you have the angled brackets, the the rounded brackets, etc. And I solved the problem. Now, there
were still other issues like the way that I was vocalizing, the way that I was naming variables, the way that I was
describing my approach, but it wasn't all over for me, right? That's what that's the important takeaway for me for
that experience. I proceeded grinding for another month to month and a half just going through lead code problems
and that's when I started applying to places that I was relatively interested in working at. One of them was
Soundhound AI or at the time it was just called Soundhound. Not I don't even remember if they added AI. Anyways, uh
Soundhound was the name of the company at the time and I remember absolutely smashing the questions that I got
largely because a bunch of them were easys and mediums that I've seen before or was able to reason through. Now,
there was this one question that I will never forget and that is the one that the lead architect asked me who I'd
essentially be working under and he asked me this in a behavioral round. He said, "Is this just a little phase for
you or are you genuinely interested in software engineering?" And that felt like a slap across the face because I
essentially had to do what most candidates do in four years in like 5 months. Now, what I really wanted to
tell him was, "Dude, would you lock yourself in a room for 7 to eight hours a day? You know, maybe taking a break
once a week for like 5 hours on a Sunday to teach yourself programming with almost zero guidance. if you didn't
absolutely feel passionate about the space. That's what I wanted to tell him, but obviously I couldn't tell him that.
Instead, what I said was, "Yeah, I find this really fun and engaging, and I see myself building a long-term career in
the space." And that was good enough for him because a day later, they sent me an offer letter. Now, honestly, I was
shocked. I was elated. And I felt like somebody finally recognized my work and dedication to the craft. But at the same
time, I was also conflicted. You see, I was conflicted because at the time I was also interviewing at another trading
firm in Chicago, a trading firm that I reached out to to see whether they have positions for somebody whose background
was more similar to mine. So, in both the BitX case and in this trading company case, I essentially hustled my
way into the position. They they didn't have an open position. I went out of my way to make one and I was finding
myself, you know, in the final stages of their interview process. So, while I was in Chicago interviewing, you know, they
flew me out, put me in a hotel. I literally had to make excuses to the Soundhound recruiter why I couldn't sign
the offer yet because he was calling me every day asking me what I intended to do. I remember one day calling him back,
elated that I was able to secure the Chicago offer. And I told him that I would be rejecting Soundhound's offer
because I wanted to see my career develop in the US where I knew that I'd be able to make progressively more
money, climb my way up the corporate ladder in an industry that to me was more rewarding and more aligned with my
goals. Now, the Soundhound offer that was in Toronto and I did not want to stay in Toronto. My biggest takeaway, by
the way, guys, from that round in Chicago, because a lot of people ask me like, "How do I how do I get over the
hurdle of that final interview?" My biggest takeaway is that these companies, they're really struggling to
find talent despite the fact that their pipeline is clogged with talent. That's because the profile guys that these
candidates or these firms are looking for. So they their ideal candidate, it's not the same profile of that applicant
sitting in their lead generation funnel. And I think the biggest two characteristics that pushed me over the
edge despite being self-taught were initiative and perseverance. The first is perseverance. Okay. I think
I showed them that I was able to commit myself deeply to something that I felt passionate about and I brought actual
examples of that perseverance when I was talking to them. For example, I was Jane Street's top puzzle solver at the time
and this is before you can, you know, spin up Fable 5 or Fable whatever and use AI to one-shot some of these Jane
Street puzzles. I think I completed nine out of 10 puzzles that year and tied with a number another member on their
leaderboard, right, for the most amount of puzzles solved. The second thing was initiative, right? First perseverance,
then initiative. So during the final round, I brought my laptop. They asked me if I had any questions for them, like
any interviewer asks at the end of a round, and I asked them, "Hey, do you want to see this 2D C++ game that I
built?" Now, this was a remake of a popular game called Cave Story, and it was written entirely in C++ using a
graphics library called SFML. I was able to answer the four W's that most of these firms are looking for you to
answer via my project creation. And those four W's are what did you do? Why did you do it? What mistakes did you
make? And what would you have done differently if you could go back in time? And after answering them, they
just sat there and they genuinely enjoyed playing the game. I think they spent like 5 minutes going through the
game, walking through levels, and talking to me about those four W's in particular. A day or two later, I had
the offer. My candidacy literally crushed almost every limiting belief that I see people today have when
they're looking to break into quant. I hear things like, "I'll need visas in a sponsorship." I needed visa sponsorship. I still got
the position. So what if you need visa sponsorship? I hear things like, "I don't have a CS degree." I never learned
CS formally. I'm self-taught. I hear things like, "I need a PhD." I didn't have a PhD. I still don't have a PhD. I
hear things like, "Well, I'm not the smartest person in the room." I wasn't either. Oh, I could never compete with
math olympiads. I'm not a math olympiad. Like, I did math in university. I took a couple of courses. That's it. And so on
and so forth. Every limiting belief I essentially shattered with my candidacy. And that's where my journey in the quant
space really began. So, let's talk about that now. I remember joining as a junior developer and my first task was to
increase the amount of logging we were performing on an application that intermittently started shutting down.
You see, the application was a parser for a popular exchange's RFQ feed. And for those of you that don't know, RFQ
stands for request for quote. So essentially, a broker will say, I want you guys to give me a quote, a bid in an
ask for this instrument. Tell me where you're at, and I might buy or sell, you know, to you given that information. We
received that information as XML data in a really janky format that was not document documented via some like
third-party data adapter. Now, I needed to study the schema, parse the legs of each trade, and categorize it as, for
example, an iron condor or a butterfly or whatever other instrument type it was classified as. You see, the way that the
quant trading space structures products is that they give you progressively harder things to do to see how much they
can push you given your current title and set of responsibilities. So, naturally, the next project that I was
going to be working on was allowing traders to create their own userdefined spreads on the CME instead of just
parsing other people's requests for quotes on instruments via ice chat. So the CME in contrast with ICE is a much
larger and more structured exch ex exchange. So naturally it was a logical extension from working on that you know
ICE instrument parsing on that front. So in this case instead of instruments being created and sent to me to parse I
have to take traders inputs via guey and create instruments on the CME in two stages. You see, when you create any
future spread or futures only related instrument on the CME, all you have to do is pick a collection of futures and
send it to the exchange and it would create that userdefined spread for you if that instrument didn't already exist.
There were only a couple of other rules like if the inverse of that future spread existed, then it would reject
your request and just ask you to trade the opposite direction of that inverse future spread. You know, a bunch of
other fancy rules. But getting back to this, anything to do with a future tied to an option or series of option had to
happen in two stages. You'd have to detect whether or not the instrument or collection of instruments that the
trader has selected contained a single future and an option in combination. If it had both of those in combination, now
the game changed a little. If it does, you'd have to create the underlying future spread first. And once you
receive confirmation from the exchange that it has been created, you then had to tack on the options to that future
spread such that the full option bearing instrument you wanted could be created. Now this project was my gateway to the
world of concurrency as a junior as it relates to quantitative development because it required you to apply a lot
of business logic on one thread while continuously receiving information from the exchange on another. My tooling work
then expanded to latency related applications like our electronic eye. Something that's very important to keep
in mind when trying to be as competitive as you want in the space as it relates to that like market scanning electronic
eye is ticktorade latency. I developed a tool that not only needed to parse PCAP data but also internal bin logs to find
trades that we made via our FPGAs. It essentially correlated market data packets that triggered that trade with
order entry requests that left our systems and then compared those two network tap timestamps, computing the
latency that resulted from them while streaming all of that information to Graphfana via Elastic Stack and Influx
DB. Fast forward a little, I started being fielded not just projects related to tooling and visualization, but also
riskrelated projects. For example, I worked on an application monitor. What is that? You see, quant trading firms
are very particular about controlling risk. They oftent times have kill switches, literal physical laptops that
a trader can interface with a small little guey. And essentially, he can shut down any application that has order
entry capabilities if they feel like it's going haywire. Now what that little guey would do is it would just connect
to one large application monitor which is something that I ended up owning in the organization. That application
monitor acts like this large server that connects to every order entry related application because those are the ones
that can make trades and can cause cascading losses. That application monitor communicates to every riskbearing order entry app. Every
single one. It's important to understand that. And I was responsible for managing that application monitor and correctly
configuring it for new applications and adding features to that application monitor whenever new forms of
quantifiable risk were introduced that should lead to us disabling a given order entry application. For instance,
if the CME's redundant fill reconciliation tool called drop copy stopped heartbeating, application monitor would pick up on it and block
all automated risk gateways associated with that drop copy fill path. Above and beyond that, I moved towards more
traderf facing risk limit generation applications, ones that would require maybe parsing XML or JSON and updating
risk limits throughout the organization. Those risk limits were compared to actual physical risk inventory that the
firm held via various portfolios and I was responsible for maintaining that risk crunching and risk calculating
application as well not just the entry path which would you know parse a JSON and turn those into actual limits. When
one metric was triggered it would send an alert to a trader's guey application that would notify him or her as to what
their risk level was. Now, I remember the frustration that I experienced sometimes interfacing with traders, not
because they're bad people, but because there would always be, you know, various do this, do that, change this, change
that, please, and everybody would have like a different opinion as to what should be changed. For example, maybe
the Slack alert, you know, was generating a sound that wasn't loud enough. Or maybe, you know, the time it
took for one risk to transition from uh orange risk to red risk or one tier to another was too long or too short. That
then expanded to exposure to market data consuming applications and market data publishing applications. For example, I
worked on a market data aggregator like tool which essentially took snapshots of our order books over time and persisted
and persisted not only our own theo calculations for futures into those one second buckets but also entire snapshots
of order books to be used to run historical back tests on. and researchers would be the primary consumer of that information in whatever
structured or unstructured database that I decided to save it in. Now, the reason that this data pipeline was needed to
begin with was because our data infrastructure pipeline wasn't robust at the time. Researchers were reading
parquet files saved on network drives and that was extremely slow. And so, in building out this data pipeline, I was
able to reduce their back test data retrieval times by 90%. And that's a massive increase in a world where being
quick and iterating even quicker is just very very very important. It then moved to market data related applications like
a resting order detector. You guys see quant firms often try to categorize orders. They do that to understand the
nature of the order flow. That categorization will provide traders with additional information that they can
then use to gain an advantage or trade against. For example, if you can classify an order with relative
certainty that it is a paper order, not a electronically submitted order, you can then act on that information. Paper
orders, they're placed manually by hedge funds, pension funds, or large retail traders. Now, being able to categorize
them, it involves a deep understanding of the market data exchange protocol that we were interfacing with alongside,
you know, trading engine related behavior. For example, you know, an insight that I garnered while reading
documentation is that orders that survive an exchange's close are usually solid enough indicators that there was a
human intention in placing those orders because they weren't pruned at the close. Whereas orders like fill or kill
or fill and kill, those sorts of orders don't even get persisted long enough for them to be classified as paper. I then
transition to build out the firm's pricing sheets. Now this is another market data consumption application but
instead of being a back-end server like uh you know the resting order detector it was now a front-end guey related uh
consumption field. So essentially traders have option class expirations and those expirations are partitioned
option series grouped by strike. Now the options pricing sheet displays various pricing volume and Greeks metrics via
graphical user interface for a series of strikes and expirations or maturities. Because the volume of data that was
being fed to these guies were so large, I needed to implement several optimizations including for example to
only subscribe to options that were in view on that particular guey. Because imagine you're subscribed to a stream of
like hundreds maybe thousands of options. That's a lot of data. It's a lot of different uh pieces of
information for your screen to draw and that'll get really slow. So for example, a trader might be subscribed to or
interested in a given maturity or given option class expiration, but their screen is only showing 20 of those 100
strikes at any given time. So instead of subscribing to Greeks or market data for an entire option class expiration at
once, you need to be able to detect when a given strike is actually in the viewport in view and then unsubscribe
from strikes that aren't and resubscribe to strikes that are as a trader, you know, goes up and down, you know, and
scrolls the option chain. Now also imagine amongst various expireies as a trader moves the window up and down he
also moves it side to side and he scrolls between expireies that he's enabled. So when an entire expiry now
leaves the page because you know the user has scrolled horizontally past it. We also need to unsubscribe from all
strikes associated with that OCE. Now by the time I reached my 4 and a half year mark at that organization, I was also
working on direct market access applications or in other words our automated marketmaking algorithms. I was
responsible for multiple layers of this application from hedging our delta to entire back-end logic loops to even
front-end development to communicate changes and take inputs to and from our traders. Applications like these guys,
they require database buildouts, guey changes, and hedging logic additions that are only given to trusted senior
developers with years of experience and years of proving themselves at these organizations. You see, you're not going
to give this level of responsibility to any developer. You need to make sure that their code is airtight, that they
know what they're doing, that they know how to test their code as well. Because imagine a rogue trading agent starts
submitting a bunch of orders. That's a recipe for disaster. Now when you start moving into this domain, now you're
working with more advanced concepts like core pinning, CPU isolation and you know Linux level API calls like task set to
be able to maintain the CPU's cache affinity. And at this level almost everything guys it's questioned and
everything is expected to be optimized. For example, I was working on the guey side with another senior developer and
while working on it from day one, I had to make sure that it was a thin client. By that I mean that we can only send and
receive the minimum amount of information to be required to control the autotrader to make sure that it only
receives the information that it needs to make decisions or rather the information that the trader needs to
view to make decisions. Now, this meant, for example, opting for incremental updates and only sending snapshots of
the state of the algorithm on key events like connections. It also involved speaking to other developers who owned
other applications that I needed to interface with like our hedging system. And it involved needing a deep
understanding of concurrency. For example, dealing with in-flight quotes, always making sure your market data path
is hot. How do you notify the main evaluation loop that new market data arrived and whatever evaluation it was
just doing, it needs to stop and restart? Think about also how you handle cases where you receive acknowledgements
for quotes that you never sent. What should your application do? Should it terminate? Should it try to reconcile
its state? How do you account for inflight quotes to begin with when the next iteration of your algorithm tells
you that, hey, the quotes you just sent that you haven't received an acknowledgement for, yeah, those were
wrong. Back out of those. we need to cancel them. And then once you've answered all of those questions, how do
you build this application in a way that's testable given some dummy test data whose form you haven't even thought
up of yet? Throughout all of this, guys, what I realized is that being strong technically is not enough for a role in
quant. You're going to be doing a lot more than coding. You're communicating. You're interacting with people. You're
managing budgets. You're managing emotions. You're leading teams, right? You're speaking to people across various
time zones. You need to coordinate your agenda, how you work, when you work, how you structure your work. Let me give you
an example. I was responsible for two internship classes and I led the hiring decisions after each internship came to
its conclusion. I had to oversee the intern summer internship projects. And if one of the interns didn't complete
their project, guess who that reflected poorly on? Yes, the intern, but also on me. During the first summer that I was
responsible for interns, I oversaw their addition of a translation layer to our internal exchange simulator application.
What is this application? It's essentially a tool that we'd spin up in our dev environment to mimic an exchange
without actually needing to connect to the CME's test net, for example. And so, initially, this internal simulator
application would use Protobuff and gRPC and communicating with our own internal tooling. But that year, my boss wanted
us to outfit that simulator-like application with the CME's simple binary encoding order entry translation layer.
In other words, he wanted that internal simulator to be configured in a way that it could accept both our messages
derived from our own internal Protobuff based protocol and the CME's formatted messages. The second year that I oversaw
interns, I actually had them work on the same application but on the other side. So they outfitted simulator to support
MDP3 which is the CME's market data layer. And all this had to be configurable via that internal simulator
applications configuration file. That first summer though in particular I also realized that a big difficulty in the
space is also about how do you as a you know quantitative developer quantitative trader quantitative researcher how do
you deliver hard information one of our interns for example he wasn't going to make the cut and wasn't going to receive
a new grad offer HR asked me do you want us to break the news or do you want to break the news yourself now I could have
taken the easy route I could have just said hey HR you know do your go talk to him. But instead, what I did was
confront what was difficult for me. I had to think of the best, most generous, and most kind way to tell somebody that,
"Listen, bro, you're just not good enough." And that was very difficult. The next day, I sat him in a room, you
know, HR was there, told him exactly what we would have wanted and where he fell short and told him that because of
that, we just couldn't extend him a return offer. And I say this not to dampen the mood, but just to communicate
how important it is to strengthen your interpersonal skills because that's a side of this industry that oftentimes
gets overlooked. During my third year, I also took on two junior developers. My boss saw that I did really good with the
interns and he's like, "All right, well, here's two new junior developers. Have fun and go mentor them." And so I
mentored them from that third year all the way to the end of my tenure at that organization. That means that we I you
know led standups, spoke to them, assigned them projects, broke down their tasks, reported their progress back to
my boss, and if they were not making progress, guess who that looked bad upon? Me, right? Above and beyond that,
I also got involved on interview panels where I would be oftent times interviewing people that were smarter
